title: Empty states, errors, and the screens teams forget
metaTitle: Empty state design for the first session
excerpt: Empty state design covers the blank screen, the first success, and the failure. Those three teach a product faster than a populated happy path.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. A new product often opens onto a screen as empty as a grid waiting for the first real item.
caption: The first open is a blank, not a demo. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an empty screen say?
faqs.answer: Name the place, say why it is empty, and offer the one action that creates the first object. A brand-new account and a filter that matches nothing are different empties. The filter case should say the filter is the reason and should let the person clear it. Sample data is fine only when it is obviously a sample and easy to remove.

faqs.question: Where should an error appear?
faqs.answer: Put it where the failure happened. A field error belongs at the field, and a failed save belongs at the action without throwing away what the person typed. Say what went wrong, whether the work is still there, and what to do next. A vanishing toast that only says error is not a designed state.

faqs.question: When in the project should these screens be designed?
faqs.answer: Design them with the populated screen, as required frames, and implement the real sentences in the same ticket. A review that only looks at a full table has not reviewed the feature. The first customer will meet the blank account long before they meet the demo data.

markdown:
Empty state design is the specification for three screens teams skip: the blank, the first success, and the failure. Those three teach the product faster than the happy path. The happy path assumes the person already understands the place and already has data. On the first visit they have neither.

A team that draws only the populated screen is designing the second week. The first session is empty, or it fails, or it is the moment something finally works. If those moments are an afterthought, the product feels unfinished at the exact time the person is deciding whether to stay. Write the three screens while the feature is still a decision, not after the demo data has made the gap invisible.

## The blank screen

The blank screen is the product introducing itself with no records to hide behind. It should name the place, say why it is empty, and offer the one action that creates the first object. "No items" is a status code spoken aloud. "No leads yet. Add the first company you are talking to." is an instruction tied to the job. The second sentence is the design.

Do not fill the blank with sample rows unless the person can tell they are samples and can remove them in one action. Fake rows that look real teach the wrong shape of the data and create cleanup. A sentence and a button are more honest, and they are faster to build than a realistic fiction.

A picture is optional. If you use one, the words still have to carry the screen for someone who does not see the picture. Keep the picture quiet. A joke that depends on the illustration will not survive contact with a tired user, and it will not survive a screen reader.

Match the blank to the cause. A new account is a different empty from a filter that matches nothing, and both differ from a search. The filter case should say the filter is why the list is clear, and it should offer to clear it. Otherwise people believe their data disappeared. That is a trust failure caused by a sentence nobody wrote. The search case should repeat the query, so they can see what produced nothing.

## The first success

The first time the action works, the person learns what the product thinks "done" means. Say what was created, where it went, and the sensible next step. This is a poor moment for a newsletter prompt or a tour of unused features. They just finished a job. Acknowledge that job.

If the object now lives in a list, show the list with the new object easy to recognize. A success banner above an unchanged empty state makes people unsure the save happened. The interface should agree with itself. One truth, visible in both the message and the list.

Use the same nouns as the button that caused the result. If the button said "Add company," the success should talk about the company. "Record created" is a different product, usually the database speaking through the interface. Consistency here is how the product starts to feel like one idea instead of a stack of components that each have their own dialect.

## The failure

Failures are part of the interface. Name what failed. Say whether the person's work is still there. Say the next action: retry, edit a field, or wait. A toast that says "Error" and disappears is a refusal to design the state. It also trains people to screenshot quickly, which is a sign the product did not keep the explanation.

Put the message at the point of failure. A field problem belongs at the field. A network problem belongs at the action they took, and it must not clear the form. Losing the typed work and the explanation in the same moment is how you teach people to keep a backup in a notes app. They will, and they will trust you less.

The W3C describes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a shared standard so content can be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Conformance is meeting the success criteria. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the document to keep beside an error that occupies the whole screen. The message has to be text. Color alone cannot carry it. The words have to be understandable without a support agent translating a code. Meeting that in the screens you call done is a quality bar. A badge added the week before launch is not a substitute for the sentence.

Design the partial failure too. One row saved and one rejected. A file that was too large. A permission the person does not have. These are ordinary, and each needs a sentence. They do not each need a unique illustration. They need the truth, including what was kept and what was not. "Some of these could not be saved" is incomplete until you say which ones.

## Specify them while you specify the happy path

In the design file, the blank, the success, and the failure sit beside the populated screen as required frames. A review that looks only at the full table has not reviewed the feature. In the build, those states are part of the component, with the real copy. A TODO where the sentence should be is a blank screen of a worse kind, because the developer's note ships if someone is careless.

Hanabi treats the three frames as part of finishing an interface, not as polish. The code is usually straightforward once the sentences exist. React components already have a place for conditional copy. The delay happens when the sentences are assigned to "content" and content is scheduled for later. Later becomes the week a real account is empty and looks broken.

Give each state an owner on the ticket. Someone writes the words. Someone implements those words, not a paraphrase invented in the pull request. Someone reads them on a fresh account before the feature is called done. That read is short. It catches the placeholder that sounded acceptable in a meeting and absurd on a phone.

Write the states in a list the whole team can see: blank, success, field error, network error, permission error. If a state cannot happen, say so, so nobody invents a message for it. If it can happen, the list is not complete until the sentence is real. This is dull work. It is also the work that makes the first session feel intentional.

## The first session is mostly these screens

A long tour is a weak substitute for a blank screen that tells the truth and a success that confirms it. People will meet your empty state before they meet your best screenshot. If you are deciding how much to explain before they have done the job, the next piece is [onboarding that respects a busy user's time](/blog/onboarding-that-respects-time). Start from the job. Let these three screens carry the teaching.

When the blank, the success, and the failure should be designed with the rest of the interface, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A path is finished only when the screens with nothing on them, and the screens where something went wrong, are as deliberate as the demo.
